title: Heal us
hookLine: names of the sick are added here in many communities

cards: Stand near someone saying the silent Amidah and, at one point, you might catch a pause, longer than usual. Their lips keep moving, but not with the printed words. If you could hear, you'd hear names.
Sarah, daughter of Miriam. David, son of Ruth. A grandmother in the hospital.
A friend's child in chemo. A coworker they barely know. The prayer book leaves a door open here, right in the middle of the prayer's fixed words.

teach.b: The eighth blessing begins with a verse from the prophet Jeremiah, who prays, in the old Jewish translation: "Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved; for Thou art my praise."
The Amidah changes one thing. Me becomes us. Heal us, and we shall be healed.
Even about illness, the prayer speaks as a group.
Then it asks for refuah shleimah, complete healing, for all our wounds, and ends: blessed are You, who heals the sick of Your people Israel.
Refuah is healing; a rofe is a doctor, and you heard the same root in Gevurot: God heals the sick.
The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, explains why healing is eighth: circumcision happens on the eighth day, and the baby needs healing after it.
And in Avodah Zarah 8a, it says that a person with someone sick at home may mention them in this blessing. So in many communities, people add names here, quietly.

teach.h: NAMES ADDED, WITH A MOTHER'S NAME.
teach.b: A common custom is to use the person's Hebrew name and their mother's name: David son of Ruth.
Some say the phrase refuah shleimah, complete healing, of body and of spirit. Notice the order of the requests: understanding, return, forgiveness, being seen, then healing.
The body gets its turn right after the heart, and it gets it every day.

how: Refa'enu is the eighth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews add a personal prayer for someone who is ill within it, naming the person by their Hebrew name and their mother's name.

games.q: your aunt is in the hospital. you're saying the weekday Amidah. where might you add her name?
o: only in the blessing for the ancestors.
games.why: the Talmud allows a personal mention of the sick in refa'enu, and many add the name there with a mother's name.

practice: Hold in mind someone who's sick right now, in body or in spirit, someone close or someone you only heard about, and say their name quietly; if you know their mother's name, you can add it, the way many Jews do.
If you pray, you can ask for their complete healing. If not, simply hold the name with care for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Refuah. Healing. The Amidah's eighth blessing, Jeremiah's prayer made plural, where names of the sick are added.

orig.note: Hebrew: complete healing. what many people say to and about the sick.
